draft.title: Map conventions
card: A good map has six parts, often remembered as BOLTSS: border, orientation, legend, title, scale and source.
Orientation and border
orientation is a north arrow, which shows which way is north. The border is a frame around the map.
Legend and scale
the legend explains what the colours and symbols mean. The scale links distance on the map to distance on the ground.
Title and source
the title says what the map shows. The source says where the information came from.
draft.remember: Each BOLTSS part answers a question a map reader might ask.

a.q: A student wants to work out how far it is between two towns on a map. Which map part should the student use?
a.why: The scale links distance on the map to distance on the ground, so it is used to find real distances. The legend is tempting because it helps a reader use the map, but it only explains symbols and colours.
a.clue: Which part links map distance to ground distance?

b.q: Priya draws a map of bus stops in her town. A classmate asks where she found the stop locations. Which part of her map should answer this?
b.why: The source says where the information came from, so it answers where the stop locations were found. The title is tempting because it describes the map, but it only says what the map shows, not where the information came from.
b.clue: Which part names where the information came from?

problems.detail: The remember line says each BOLTSS part answers a question a map reader might ask. The card never presents the parts this way, and the border (a frame) does not clearly answer any reader's question, so the line adds a framing the card does not support.

check.summary: Facts and both questions are sound. The only issue is a remember line that frames every BOLTSS part as answering a reader's question, which the card does not teach and which does not fit the border.
